title: World Politics: The End of Bipolarity

topics.title: The Berlin Wall falls: end of a bipolar world

learn.hook: For 28 years a concrete wall cut one city in two. On a November night in 1989, ordinary Berliners climbed it with hammers, and an entire world order began to crack.
points: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961 to separate communist East Berlin from capitalist West Berlin. It became the most visible symbol of the Cold War divide between the two blocs.
In November 1989 crowds broke down the Wall. Its fall is remembered as the moment the Cold War began to end.
The two parts of Germany were unified in 1990, and in 1991 the Soviet Union itself broke up.
Bipolar world: two superpowers (USA and USSR) and their blocs dominate world politics. Unipolar world: a single superpower dominates.
The disintegration of the USSR ended the bipolar system and left the USA as the only superpower.

example.q: Arrange and explain: Why do textbooks treat the fall of the Berlin Wall as the start of the end of bipolarity?
steps: The Wall (1961) physically divided a city between the two rival blocs.
Its fall (November 1989) showed that people in the Soviet bloc were rejecting communist rule.
Germany reunified in 1990, removing the front line of the Cold War in Europe.
The USSR broke up in 1991, so only one superpower remained.
example.answer: Because the Wall was the symbol of the two-bloc divide, its fall marked the collapse of that divide, completed by the Soviet break-up in 1991.

learn.reallife: Pieces of the Berlin Wall are displayed in many countries as reminders that walls built by politics can fall. India itself had to rethink its foreign policy after 1991, when its old partner, the USSR, disappeared.

games.title: Match the term
pairs: Two superpowers and their blocs dominate
Symbol of the Cold War divide

quiz.q: In which year was the Berlin Wall built?
quiz.explain: The Wall went up in 1961 and stood until 1989.
steps: Asked: the year the Berlin Wall was built, not the year it fell.
Fact: the Wall was built in 1961 to separate East Berlin from West Berlin.
1989 is the year it fell, so it is a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 1961
quiz.mistake: Confuses the year of building with the year of its fall

quiz.q: The fall of the Berlin Wall took place in:
quiz.explain: Crowds broke through the Wall in November 1989.
steps: Asked: when the Wall fell.
Fact: crowds broke down the Wall in November 1989.
1990 was German unification and 1991 the Soviet break-up, so they do not fit.
Answer: November 1989
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the Wall's fall with German unification or the Soviet break-up

quiz.q: What did the Berlin Wall symbolise?
options: The border between Germany and the USSR
The end of the Second World War
The division between the capitalist and communist worlds
A trade barrier inside the European Union
quiz.explain: It divided East and West Berlin and stood for the Cold War split between the two blocs.
steps: Asked: what the Wall stood for.
Fact: it divided communist East Berlin from capitalist West Berlin.
So it was the most visible symbol of the Cold War split between the two blocs.
Answer: The division between the capitalist and communist worlds
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Wall was an international border with the USSR

quiz.q: A world in which two superpowers and their alliances dominate international politics is called:
quiz.explain: 'Bi' means two; the Cold War world was bipolar.
steps: Asked: the name for a world dominated by two superpowers and their blocs.
'Bi' means two; the USA and USSR led the two blocs.
So such a world is bipolar (unipolar means one superpower).
Answer: Bipolar
quiz.mistake: Confuses bipolar with multipolar

quiz.q: Which event completed the end of the bipolar world order?
options: Disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991
quiz.explain: Once the USSR broke up, only one superpower remained.
steps: Asked: which event completed the end of bipolarity.
Bipolarity needs two superpowers; it ended only when one of them ceased to exist.
The USSR disintegrated in 1991, leaving only the USA.
Answer: Disintegration of the Soviet Union in 1991
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Wall's fall alone ended bipolarity

quiz.q: The two parts of Germany were unified in:
quiz.explain: Unification came in 1990, a year after the Wall fell.
steps: Asked: the year of German unification.
Fact: the two parts of Germany were unified in 1990.
This was a year after the Wall fell in 1989.
Answer: 1990
quiz.mistake: Assumes unification happened the same year the Wall fell

quiz.q: Assertion (A): After 1991 the world was often described as unipolar. Reason (R): The disintegration of the USSR left the USA as the only superpower.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true, and the end of the USSR is exactly why the world came to be seen as unipolar.
steps: A: true — after 1991 the world was often called unipolar.
R: true — the USSR's disintegration left the USA as the only superpower.
R explains A: one superpower is exactly what 'unipolar' means.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to link the Soviet collapse with the new unipolar order

quiz.q: Case: A student writes, 'The Berlin Wall separated East Germany from Poland.' What is the correct correction?
options: It separated West Germany from France
It separated East Berlin from West Berlin
It separated the USSR from China
It separated East Germany from Austria
quiz.explain: The Wall ran through Berlin, cutting the city into a communist East and a capitalist West.
steps: The student's claim: the Wall separated East Germany from Poland.
Fact: the Wall ran through the city of Berlin, not along a national border.
So the correct statement is that it separated East Berlin from West Berlin.
Answer: It separated East Berlin from West Berlin
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Wall was a national border rather than a wall within a city

teach.ask: Gappu flutters in: 'Why does everyone say a wall falling ended a whole world system? Walls fall all the time!'
teach.praise: Chirp! So the Wall stood for the two-bloc divide, and when it fell and the USSR broke up, the world went from two superpowers to one!
teach.nudge: Nice start. But what did the Wall stand for, and how many superpowers were left in the end?

revise.summary: The Berlin Wall (built 1961) symbolised the Cold War divide; its fall in November 1989 began the end of the bipolar world, completed when the USSR broke up in 1991, leaving the USA as the only superpower.
focus: Dates: Wall built 1961, fell November 1989, Germany unified 1990, USSR broke up 1991
Meaning of bipolar and unipolar world
Why the Soviet break-up ended bipolarity
remember: Berlin Wall separated communist East Berlin from capitalist West Berlin
Bipolar: two superpowers (USA and USSR) and their blocs dominate
Unipolar: a single superpower dominates
traps: Don't confuse the year the Wall was built (1961) with the year it fell (1989).
The Wall was within Berlin, not a national border.
The Wall's fall alone did not end bipolarity; the USSR's break-up in 1991 did.

learn.hook: Imagine a country where the state owns every factory and farm, there is no unemployment, and one party runs everything. That was the Soviet Union for over 70 years.
points: The USSR (Union of Soviet Socialist Republics) came into being after the socialist revolution in Russia in 1917, led by the Bolsheviks. It was inspired by socialist ideals and aimed at an egalitarian society.

After the Second World War, the East European countries freed by the Soviet army came under its control. This group was called the Second World or the socialist bloc, and the Warsaw Pact was its military alliance.
Key features: state ownership and control of productive assets, a centrally planned economy, and the dominance of the Communist Party, with no other parties allowed.
Achievements: the USSR became a great power with a strong industrial base, large energy resources, a vast communications network and a powerful military.
The state ensured a minimum standard of living: subsidised health, education and childcare, and no unemployment.

example.q: Classify: Which of these are features of the Soviet system? (a) Many competing parties (b) State ownership of productive assets (c) Central planning (d) Free market prices
steps: Many competing parties: no, only the Communist Party was allowed.
State ownership of productive assets: yes.
Central planning: yes, the state planned production.
Free market prices: no, the state controlled the economy.

learn.reallife: India's Planning Commission (1950) drew some inspiration from Soviet-style planning, though India kept democracy and a mixed economy. Steel plants like Bhilai were built with Soviet help.

items.text: The USSR was born after the socialist revolution of ___.
The military alliance of the Soviet bloc was the ___ Pact.
The East European countries in the Soviet bloc were called the ___ World.
The Soviet economy was planned and controlled by the ___.

quiz.q: The Soviet Union came into being after the socialist revolution in Russia in:
quiz.explain: The Bolshevik-led revolution of 1917 created the Soviet state.
steps: Asked: the year of the socialist revolution that created the USSR.
Fact: the Bolshevik-led revolution in Russia took place in 1917.
1945 is the end of the Second World War, so it does not fit.
Answer: 1917
quiz.mistake: Confuses the revolution with later dates such as the end of WWII

quiz.q: Which military alliance bound the Soviet bloc countries together?
quiz.explain: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the Soviet bloc; NATO was the Western alliance.
steps: Asked: the military alliance of the Soviet bloc.
Fact: the Warsaw Pact was the Soviet bloc's alliance.
NATO was the Western alliance, the rival bloc.
Answer: Warsaw Pact
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the rival Cold War alliances

quiz.q: The 'Second World' referred to:
options: The developing countries of Asia and Africa
The USA and its Western allies
The socialist bloc of East European countries led by the USSR
quiz.explain: The First World was the Western bloc, the Second World the Soviet bloc, and the Third World the developing countries.
steps: The Cold War world was split into First, Second and Third Worlds.
First = Western bloc; Third = developing countries.
So the Second World was the socialist bloc of East European countries led by the USSR.
Answer: The socialist bloc of East European countries led by the USSR
quiz.mistake: Confuses Second World with Third World

quiz.q: Which was NOT a feature of the Soviet political system?
quiz.explain: Only the Communist Party was allowed, so there was no multi-party competition.
steps: Asked: which was NOT part of the Soviet political system.
Features: Communist Party dominance, state control of the economy, central planning.
No other parties were allowed, so competition among several parties was NOT a feature.
Answer: Competition among several political parties
quiz.mistake: Assumes every big country has multi-party elections

quiz.q: Which achievement is correctly linked to the Soviet system?
options: Ensuring a minimum standard of living with no unemployment
Producing the world's best consumer goods
Running the most open economy in the world
quiz.explain: The state guaranteed basic needs and jobs, though consumer goods were of lower quality than in the West.
steps: Asked: a real achievement of the Soviet system.
Fact: the state ensured a minimum standard of living — subsidised health and education, no unemployment.
It did not have the best consumer goods, a free press or an open economy.
Answer: Ensuring a minimum standard of living with no unemployment
quiz.mistake: Credits the USSR with Western-style consumer quality or freedoms

quiz.q: In the Soviet economy, who owned and controlled productive assets such as land and factories?
quiz.explain: Productive assets were owned and controlled by the state, and the economy was planned.
steps: Asked: who owned land and factories in the USSR.
Fact: a key feature was state ownership and control of productive assets.
So the state owned them, not private firms or foreign investors.
Answer: The state
quiz.mistake: Thinks socialist means community or private ownership

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The Soviet Union became a great power after the Second World War. Reason (R): It had a strong industrial base, large energy resources and a powerful military.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both are true and R explains A: its industrial and military strength made it a superpower.
steps: A: true — the USSR became a great power after the Second World War.
R: true — it had a strong industrial base, energy resources and a powerful military.
R explains A: that strength is what made it a superpower.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why the USSR counted as a superpower

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The Soviet system allowed many parties to compete in elections. Reason (R): The Soviet state subsidised health care and education.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false because only the Communist Party was allowed. R is true: welfare services were subsidised.
steps: A: false — only the Communist Party was allowed; no multi-party elections.
R: true — the state subsidised health care and education.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Assumes welfare provision implies democracy

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: 'Soviet system, Soviet system... but what WAS it? Who owned things and who ruled?'
teach.praise: Tweet tweet! The state owned and planned everything, one party ruled, and everyone got a job and basic needs. Got it!
teach.nudge: Good. But who ran the government, and what did the system promise ordinary people?

revise.summary: The USSR arose from the 1917 Bolshevik revolution. Its system had state ownership, central planning and one-party rule; it became a great power and guaranteed a minimum standard of living.
focus: Features of the Soviet political and economic system
Second World and the Warsaw Pact
remember: USSR formed after the socialist revolution of 1917, led by the Bolsheviks
Second World = socialist bloc; Warsaw Pact = its military alliance
Features: state ownership, centrally planned economy, Communist Party dominance
traps: The Soviet system did not allow multi-party competition.
Welfare provision does not mean democracy.
The Warsaw Pact was the Soviet alliance; NATO was the Western one.

topics.title: Cracks in the system and Gorbachev's reforms

learn.hook: The USSR could launch rockets into space, yet shoppers queued for hours for bread and shoes. By the 1980s, something had to give.
points: The system became bureaucratic and authoritarian. There was no freedom of speech, and the one-party rule of the Communist Party was not accountable to the people.
The USSR fell behind the West in technology and infrastructure (for example, computers), and consumer goods were scarce.
Russia dominated the other republics, and people in other regions felt neglected and suppressed.
The arms race with the US and the cost of supporting satellite states drained resources. The 1979 intervention in Afghanistan weakened the system further.
Mikhail Gorbachev became General Secretary of the Communist Party in 1985. His reforms were perestroika (restructuring of the economy) and glasnost (openness, more freedom of expression).

example.q: A newspaper in 1987 Moscow prints open criticism of the government for the first time. Which reform does this reflect, and why?
steps: Perestroika means restructuring the economy.
Glasnost means openness: more freedom to speak and publish.
Open criticism in a newspaper is about freedom of expression.

learn.reallife: Like a company that keeps old machines too long, the Soviet economy lost out in the computer age. Indian IT firms grew in the 1990s precisely when that technology gap had become huge.

games.title: True or false?
items: The Soviet system allowed open criticism of the government before Gorbachev.
There was no freedom of speech; criticism was suppressed.
The USSR lagged behind the West in technology such as computers.
The book notes its technological and infrastructure lag.
Russia dominated the other Soviet republics.
People in other regions felt neglected and suppressed.
Glasnost means restructuring of the economy.
Glasnost means openness; perestroika means restructuring.
The 1979 Afghanistan intervention strengthened the Soviet economy.
It drained resources and weakened the system.

quiz.q: Mikhail Gorbachev became the General Secretary of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union in:
quiz.explain: He took charge in 1985 and launched reforms.
steps: Asked: when Gorbachev became General Secretary.
Fact: he took charge of the Communist Party in 1985 and began reforms.
1989 (Wall falls) and 1991 (break-up) came later.
Answer: 1985
quiz.mistake: Confuses his rise with the fall of the Wall or the break-up

quiz.q: 'Perestroika' refers to:
quiz.explain: Perestroika was the economic restructuring reform; glasnost was openness.
steps: Gorbachev had two reforms: perestroika and glasnost.
Perestroika = restructuring of the economy; glasnost = openness.
So perestroika means restructuring.
Answer: Restructuring
quiz.mistake: Swaps the meanings of perestroika and glasnost

quiz.q: 'Glasnost' refers to:
quiz.explain: Glasnost allowed more freedom of speech and information.
steps: Gorbachev's two reforms: perestroika and glasnost.
Glasnost = openness, more freedom of expression; perestroika = restructuring.
So glasnost means openness.
Answer: Openness
quiz.mistake: Swaps the meanings of the two reforms

quiz.q: Which of these was a major weakness of the Soviet system?
options: Lack of democracy and freedom of speech
quiz.explain: The system was authoritarian and stifled free expression; it actually had a strong military and no unemployment.
steps: Asked: a real weakness of the Soviet system.
Fact: the system was authoritarian, with no freedom of speech and one-party rule.
It had no unemployment and a strong military, and only one party — so lack of democracy fits.
Answer: Lack of democracy and freedom of speech
quiz.mistake: Picks a problem the USSR did not have

quiz.q: Which event of 1979 drained Soviet resources and weakened the system?
quiz.explain: The Afghanistan intervention was costly and weakened the USSR.
steps: Asked: the 1979 event that drained Soviet resources.
Fact: the 1979 intervention in Afghanistan weakened the system further.
The Wall fell in 1989, so that choice has the wrong year.
Answer: Intervention in Afghanistan
quiz.mistake: Picks a Cold War event from the wrong year

quiz.q: Why did people in many Soviet republics feel neglected?
options: They had more power than Russia
They had no communist party branches
Russia dominated the Union and their regions were suppressed
quiz.explain: Of the fifteen republics, Russia dominated; others felt their identities and interests were ignored.
steps: Asked: why people in many republics felt neglected.
Fact: Russia dominated the other republics.
So people elsewhere felt their regions were neglected and suppressed.
Answer: Russia dominated the Union and their regions were suppressed
quiz.mistake: Thinks all republics had equal influence

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Gorbachev introduced glasnost. Reason (R): He wanted to reform the system by allowing greater openness and debate.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and R explains why glasnost was launched.
steps: A: true — Gorbachev introduced glasnost.
R: true — he wanted to reform the system with more openness and debate.
R explains A: reform through openness is why glasnost was launched.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Thinks Gorbachev wanted to end the USSR rather than reform it

quiz.q: Case: A Soviet citizen in 1984 could get free schooling and a job, but waited years for a car and could not criticise the government. Which pair best describes this?
options: Basic welfare guaranteed, but consumer shortages and no freedom
quiz.explain: The system secured basic needs but suffered shortages and denied political freedom.
steps: The case shows free schooling and a job: basic welfare was guaranteed.
It also shows years of waiting for a car and no right to criticise: shortages and no freedom.
So both sides together: basic welfare guaranteed, but consumer shortages and no freedom.
Answer: Basic welfare guaranteed, but consumer shortages and no freedom
quiz.mistake: Overlooks either the achievements or the weaknesses of the system

teach.ask: Gappu frowns: 'If the Soviet Union was so strong, why did it need fixing? And what were those two Russian words?'
teach.praise: Hoot! It lacked freedom, fell behind in technology and spent too much on arms, so Gorbachev tried perestroika and glasnost!
teach.nudge: You've told me the problems. Now what did Gorbachev do in 1985 to fix them?

revise.summary: The Soviet system became bureaucratic and authoritarian, lagged in technology and consumer goods, and was drained by the arms race and Afghanistan (1979). Gorbachev (1985) launched perestroika and glasnost.
remember: Gorbachev became General Secretary in 1985
Perestroika = restructuring of the economy
Glasnost = openness, more freedom of expression
traps: Don't swap perestroika (restructuring) and glasnost (openness).
The USSR had no unemployment and a strong military; its weakness was lack of democracy.
Gorbachev wanted to reform the system, not end it.

topics.title: 1989 to 1991: the Soviet Union comes apart

learn.hook: In August 1991 tanks rolled into Moscow to stop reform. Within four months the country those tanks belonged to no longer existed.
points: In 1989 people in East European countries (part of the Soviet bloc) rose up and overthrew their communist governments. The USSR did not intervene.

In 1991 a coup was attempted by Communist Party hardliners who opposed the reforms. It failed, and Boris Yeltsin, who had won a popular election as President of Russia, emerged as a national hero by opposing it.
In December 1991, under Yeltsin's leadership, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus (three major republics) declared that the USSR was dissolved. The Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) was formed.
Russia was accepted as the successor state of the USSR. It inherited the Soviet seat as a permanent member of the UN Security Council and took over the USSR's international treaties and commitments.

example.q: Order these events: (a) Hardliners' coup fails (b) Gorbachev comes to power (c) East European communist governments fall (d) USSR dissolved, CIS formed
steps: (b) 1985: Gorbachev comes to power.
(c) 1989: East European communist regimes fall.
(a) 1991 (August): coup attempt fails.
(d) December 1991: USSR dissolved and CIS formed.

learn.reallife: When a company is broken up, one unit usually keeps the brand and the seat on industry bodies. Russia did the same with the USSR's UN Security Council seat.

games.title: Order the collapse
items: Communist regimes in Eastern Europe fall

items.text: The republics that declared the end of the USSR in 1991 were Russia, Ukraine and ___.
The leader who emerged as a hero by opposing the 1991 coup was Boris ___.
After 1991, the ___ took the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council.
The association formed after the USSR ended was the Commonwealth of Independent ___.

quiz.q: Which three republics declared the dissolution of the USSR in December 1991?
quiz.explain: Under Yeltsin, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus announced that the USSR was dissolved.
steps: Asked: the three republics that declared the USSR dissolved in December 1991.
Fact: under Yeltsin, Russia, Ukraine and Belarus made the declaration.
The Baltic states had already broken away, so they are the tempting wrong choice.
Answer: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus
quiz.mistake: Names the Baltic states, which had already broken away

quiz.q: The 1991 coup in the USSR was attempted by:
options: Communist Party hardliners opposed to reform
quiz.explain: Hardliners tried to reverse Gorbachev's reforms; the coup failed.
steps: Asked: who attempted the 1991 coup.
Fact: Communist Party hardliners who opposed Gorbachev's reforms tried it.
It failed; reformers and NATO were not behind it.
Answer: Communist Party hardliners opposed to reform
quiz.mistake: Thinks the coup came from the reformist side

quiz.q: Who emerged as a national hero by opposing the 1991 coup?
quiz.explain: Yeltsin, the elected President of Russia, led the resistance to the coup.
steps: Asked: who became a national hero by opposing the coup.
Fact: Boris Yeltsin, elected President of Russia, led the resistance.
Gorbachev was held by the plotters, so he was not the hero.
Answer: Boris Yeltsin
quiz.mistake: Credits Gorbachev, who was actually held by the plotters

quiz.q: What was formed in place of the USSR in December 1991?
quiz.explain: The CIS was set up as a loose association of former Soviet republics.
steps: Asked: what replaced the USSR in December 1991.
Fact: the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS) was formed.
The EU and the Warsaw Pact are different bodies.
Answer: Commonwealth of Independent States
quiz.mistake: Confuses the CIS with other regional bodies

quiz.q: After the break-up, which state inherited the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council?
quiz.explain: Russia was accepted as the successor state and took the permanent seat.
steps: Asked: who took the Soviet seat in the UN Security Council.
Fact: Russia was accepted as the successor state of the USSR.
So Russia inherited the permanent seat.
Answer: Russia
quiz.mistake: Thinks the seat was shared or given to another republic

quiz.q: In 1989, what happened in East European countries of the Soviet bloc?
quiz.explain: Mass protests brought down communist regimes in 1989, and the USSR did not intervene.
steps: Asked: what happened in Eastern Europe in 1989.
Fact: people rose up and overthrew their communist governments.
The USSR did not intervene; the bloc weakened, it did not grow.
Answer: People overthrew their communist governments
quiz.mistake: Thinks the Soviet bloc grew stronger in 1989

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Russia took over the international treaties of the USSR. Reason (R): Russia was accepted as the successor state of the Soviet Union.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; as successor state Russia inherited the USSR's seat and treaty commitments.
steps: A: true — Russia took over the USSR's international treaties.
R: true — Russia was accepted as the successor state.
R explains A: as successor it inherited the treaties and commitments.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect successor status with treaty obligations

quiz.q: How many years after Gorbachev took charge did the USSR dissolve?
quiz.explain: Gorbachev took charge in 1985 and the USSR was dissolved in December 1991: 1991 - 1985 = 6.
steps: Gorbachev: 1985
Dissolution: 1991
Answer: 6
quiz.mistake: Uses 1989 (the Wall's fall) instead of 1991

teach.ask: Gappu looks confused: 'So who actually ended the Soviet Union? Did it just vanish?'
teach.praise: Squawk! After a failed hardliner coup, Yeltsin's Russia, Ukraine and Belarus ended the USSR, made the CIS, and Russia took its UN seat!
teach.nudge: Okay, but which republics signed the end, and who got the USSR's place in the UN?

revise.summary: In 1989 East Europeans overthrew communist governments; in 1991 a hardliners' coup failed and Yeltsin emerged a hero. In December 1991 Russia, Ukraine and Belarus dissolved the USSR and formed the CIS; Russia became the successor state.
focus: Sequence of events from 1985 to December 1991
Role of Yeltsin and the failed coup
remember: Russia, Ukraine and Belarus declared the USSR dissolved in December 1991
CIS = Commonwealth of Independent States
Russia inherited the USSR's UN Security Council seat and treaties
traps: The coup came from hardliners, not reformers.
The Baltic states did not make the December 1991 declaration.
Yeltsin, not Gorbachev, became the hero of the coup's failure.

topics.title: Why did the Soviet Union disintegrate?

learn.hook: A superpower with nuclear weapons and a huge army collapsed without losing a war. Explaining why is one of the favourite long answers in the board exam.
points: Internal weaknesses of political and economic institutions failed to meet people's aspirations. This is the most common explanation.
Economic stagnation over many years caused severe consumer shortages. The arms race and the cost of the satellite states in Eastern Europe and the Central Asian republics drained resources.
As information spread, ordinary citizens realised how far the USSR lagged behind the West. Gorbachev's reforms raised expectations but could not satisfy them quickly.
Gorbachev was opposed from both sides: reformers felt he was too slow, while Communist Party members and hardliners felt he was destroying the system.

Nationalism and the desire for sovereignty grew in the republics. It was strongest in the European and relatively prosperous parts, such as the Baltic states (Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania), Ukraine and Georgia.

example.q: A board question asks for two economic and one political reason for the Soviet collapse. Build the answer.
steps: Economic 1: long stagnation leading to consumer shortages.
Economic 2: huge spending on the arms race and on satellite states.
Political: a rigid, unaccountable one-party system, and rising nationalism in the republics.
example.answer: Stagnation and shortages; cost of the arms race and satellite states; an authoritarian system facing nationalist demands

learn.reallife: Just as a cricket team can lose when the dressing room splits into camps, Gorbachev lost support from both the reformers and the old guard at the same time.

games.title: True or false?
items: Nationalist demands were strongest in the poorer Central Asian republics.
They were strongest in the European and relatively prosperous regions such as the Baltics and Ukraine.
Gorbachev's reforms raised expectations they could not quickly satisfy.
They opposed them and even tried a coup.
The arms race drained Soviet resources.
Military spending left less for consumer needs.

quiz.q: According to the most common explanation, the Soviet Union disintegrated mainly because of:
options: Internal weaknesses of its political and economic institutions
quiz.explain: The system failed to meet people's aspirations; it was not defeated militarily.
steps: Asked: the most common explanation of the Soviet collapse.
Fact: internal weaknesses of political and economic institutions failed to meet people's aspirations.
The USSR was not defeated in war or invaded.
Answer: Internal weaknesses of its political and economic institutions
quiz.mistake: Assumes superpowers only collapse after military defeat

quiz.q: In which regions of the USSR was the nationalist desire for sovereignty strongest?
options: The Baltic states, Ukraine and Georgia
quiz.explain: The European and relatively prosperous regions led the push for independence.
steps: Asked: where nationalism was strongest.
Fact: it was strongest in the European and relatively prosperous parts.
These were the Baltic states, Ukraine and Georgia.
Answer: The Baltic states, Ukraine and Georgia
quiz.mistake: Assumes poorer regions pushed hardest for separation

quiz.q: Which is an ECONOMIC reason for the Soviet collapse?
quiz.explain: Shortages and stagnation are economic; the others are political.
steps: Asked: an ECONOMIC reason.
Nationalism, the coup and lack of free speech are political reasons.
Stagnation and severe consumer shortages are economic.
Answer: Stagnation and severe consumer shortages
quiz.mistake: Mixes political and economic causes

quiz.q: Why did Gorbachev's reforms fail to save the USSR?
options: They raised expectations they could not meet and were opposed by both reformers and hardliners
They were imposed by the USA
quiz.explain: Reformers found them too slow, hardliners found them too radical.
steps: Asked: why the reforms failed to save the USSR.
Fact: they raised expectations that could not be met quickly.
Reformers found them too slow and hardliners too radical, so both sides opposed him.
Answer: They raised expectations they could not meet and were opposed by both reformers and hardliners
quiz.mistake: Thinks the reforms had universal support

quiz.q: Which three countries are the Baltic states?
quiz.explain: The three Baltic republics on the Baltic Sea were among the first to push for independence.
steps: Asked: the three Baltic states.
Fact: they are Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, on the Baltic Sea.
Ukraine, Belarus and Moldova, or Poland, Hungary and Romania, are not Baltic states.
Answer: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania
quiz.mistake: Confuses the Baltics with other former Soviet or East European states

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Many Soviet citizens became openly dissatisfied in the 1980s. Reason (R): Greater openness let them learn how far the USSR lagged behind the West.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and R explains A: once information flowed, the gap with the West became obvious.
steps: A: true — many citizens became openly dissatisfied in the 1980s.
R: true — greater openness showed how far the USSR lagged behind the West.
R explains A: learning about the gap caused the dissatisfaction.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Misses the link between openness and public dissatisfaction

quiz.q: Assertion (A): The cost of the arms race was one reason for the Soviet collapse. Reason (R): The Soviet economy was the largest and most productive in the world in the 1980s.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true. R is false: the Soviet economy was stagnating and lagging behind the West.
steps: A: true — the cost of the arms race drained Soviet resources.
R: false — the Soviet economy was stagnating and lagging behind the West.
So A is true, but R is false.
Answer: A is true, but R is false
quiz.mistake: Overrates the late Soviet economy

quiz.q: Case: A Ukrainian student in 1990 says, 'We want our own government and our own language in schools.' This reflects which cause of the Soviet collapse?
options: Rise of nationalism and demands for sovereignty
quiz.explain: Demands for self-rule in republics were a major cause of the break-up.
steps: The student wants 'our own government and our own language'.
That is a demand for self-rule by a republic.
It reflects the rise of nationalism and demands for sovereignty (shock therapy came after 1991).
Answer: Rise of nationalism and demands for sovereignty
quiz.mistake: Confuses a cause of collapse with a later policy such as shock therapy

teach.ask: Gappu asks: 'Nobody conquered the Soviet Union, so why did it fall apart? Give me the reasons!'
teach.praise: Chirrup! A weak economy, a rigid system, reforms that disappointed everyone, and republics wanting freedom. That explains it!
teach.nudge: You gave me the economy. What about the republics and their demands?

revise.summary: The USSR collapsed mainly from internal weaknesses: stagnation and shortages, the cost of the arms race and satellite states, reforms that raised unmet expectations, and nationalism strongest in the Baltic states, Ukraine and Georgia.
focus: Economic and political causes of the collapse
remember: Most common explanation: internal weaknesses of political and economic institutions
Baltic states: Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania
Gorbachev was opposed by both reformers and hardliners
traps: The USSR was not defeated militarily.
Don't mix economic causes (stagnation, shortages) with political ones (nationalism, no free speech).
The late Soviet economy was stagnating, not the world's most productive.

learn.hook: In 1991 the world map gained fifteen countries, lost a superpower and changed its economic rulebook almost overnight.
points: The Cold War confrontation ended. The ideological dispute between capitalism and socialism, and with it the arms race, came to an end.
Power relations changed: the USA became the sole superpower, giving a unipolar world. Some saw this as the triumph of capitalism.
Capitalism and liberal democracy became the dominant models. The World Bank and IMF became powerful advisers to many countries.
New countries emerged: the Baltic states, East European countries and Central Asian republics. Many East European and Baltic states sought to join the European Union and NATO.

example.q: Identify the consequence: 'After 1991, advisers from the IMF and World Bank shaped the economic policies of many post-communist states.'
steps: This is about which economic model spread.
It shows capitalism becoming dominant and the growing influence of global financial institutions.
example.answer: Dominance of capitalism and greater influence of the IMF and World Bank

learn.reallife: The 1991 shift reached India too: with the USSR gone and a balance of payments crisis at home, India launched its own economic reforms the same year.

games.title: Consequence or not?
items: Greater influence of IMF and World Bank

games.title: Match the consequence to its type

quiz.q: Which of these was a consequence of the disintegration of the USSR?
options: End of the Cold War arms race
quiz.explain: The collapse ended the rivalry and the arms race; the other events came much earlier.
steps: Asked: a consequence of the Soviet break-up.
The Cold War start, the Warsaw Pact and the Berlin Wall all came long before 1991.
With the rivalry over, the arms race ended — that is a consequence.
Answer: End of the Cold War arms race
quiz.mistake: Mixes causes and early Cold War events with consequences

quiz.q: After 1991 the world was described as unipolar because:
options: The UN became a world government
China and the USA shared power equally
The USA was left as the only superpower
quiz.explain: With the USSR gone, the USA dominated alone.
steps: Unipolar means one power dominates.
After 1991 the USSR was gone and only one superpower was left.
So the world was unipolar because the USA was the only superpower.
Answer: The USA was left as the only superpower
quiz.mistake: Confuses unipolar with multipolar

quiz.q: Which institutions became powerful advisers to many countries after 1991?
quiz.explain: These institutions promoted capitalist reforms in post-communist states.
steps: Asked: institutions that advised many countries after 1991.
Fact: capitalism became dominant, and the World Bank and IMF became powerful advisers.
The Warsaw Pact and Comecon belonged to the old Soviet bloc.
Answer: World Bank and IMF
quiz.mistake: Names regional or humanitarian bodies

quiz.q: Which group of new states emerged from the former Soviet Union?
options: Central Asian republics such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan
quiz.explain: Central Asian and Baltic republics became independent states.
steps: Asked: new states that emerged from the former USSR.
Fact: the Baltic states and Central Asian republics became independent.
Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan are Central Asian republics; Indonesia or Spain were never Soviet.
Answer: Central Asian republics such as Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan
quiz.mistake: Names countries that were never Soviet republics

quiz.q: Many Baltic and East European states wanted to join which organisations after the Cold War?
quiz.explain: They wanted closer ties with Western Europe for economic and security reasons.
steps: Asked: which organisations Baltic and East European states wanted to join.
Fact: many sought to join the European Union and NATO.
They did not want to revive Soviet-era bodies like the Warsaw Pact.
Answer: European Union and NATO
quiz.mistake: Thinks they rejoined Soviet-era bodies

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Some observers saw the end of the USSR as a triumph of capitalism. Reason (R): Capitalism and liberal democracy became the dominant models after 1991.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the spread of capitalism after 1991 is why some called it a triumph.
steps: A: true — some saw the end of the USSR as the triumph of capitalism.
R: true — capitalism and liberal democracy became the dominant models.
R explains A: the spread of capitalism is why it was called a triumph.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to connect the dominance of capitalism with the 'triumph' view

quiz.q: Which statement about power after 1991 is correct?
options: Power shifted to the Warsaw Pact
The balance of power shifted in favour of the USA
No country had any military strength left
quiz.explain: With its rival gone, the US was the dominant power.
steps: Fact: after 1991 the USA became the sole superpower.
Russia did not become an equal superpower, and the Warsaw Pact ended.
So the balance of power shifted in favour of the USA.
Answer: The balance of power shifted in favour of the USA
quiz.mistake: Thinks Russia simply replaced the USSR as an equal superpower

quiz.q: Case: In 1992, Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have new flags and seats at the UN. Which consequence of the Soviet collapse does this show?
quiz.explain: The break-up created many new sovereign states.
steps: The case: Lithuania, Latvia and Estonia have new flags and UN seats.
These Baltic states became sovereign after the Soviet break-up.
So it shows the emergence of new independent countries.
Answer: Emergence of new independent countries
quiz.mistake: Picks a consequence opposite to what happened

teach.ask: Gappu chirps: 'So the Soviet Union ended. Big deal! What actually changed for the world?'
teach.praise: Wheee! The Cold War ended, the US stood alone, capitalism spread and new countries were born. The world changed!
teach.nudge: Good. Did any new countries appear on the map? And who became the only superpower?

revise.summary: The Soviet collapse ended the Cold War and the arms race, left the USA as sole superpower, made capitalism and liberal democracy dominant with the World Bank and IMF as advisers, and created new states.
focus: New states and their wish to join the EU and NATO
remember: End of the ideological dispute and the arms race
USA became the sole superpower: unipolar world
World Bank and IMF became powerful advisers
traps: Don't list earlier Cold War events as consequences.
Russia did not become an equal superpower after 1991.

learn.hook: Picture switching a whole country's economy from 'the state owns everything' to 'the market decides' in a few months. Russia tried exactly that in the 1990s.
points: Shock therapy was the model of sudden transition from an authoritarian socialist system to a democratic capitalist system, adopted in Russia, Central Asia and Eastern Europe.
It was influenced by the World Bank and the IMF. Private ownership was to be the main pattern of ownership of property.

Its elements were privatisation of state assets, corporate ownership patterns, collective farms replaced by private farming, free trade, foreign direct investment, financial openness and currency convertibility.
It also broke up the old trade alliances of the Soviet bloc and redirected trade towards the West.

The privatisation was called 'the largest garage sale in history', because valuable state industries were sold to private individuals and companies at very low prices, often far below their real value.

example.q: Which of these is NOT part of shock therapy? (a) privatisation (b) currency convertibility (c) stronger collective farms (d) free trade
steps: Shock therapy replaced collective farms with private farming.
So strengthening collective farms goes against it.
Privatisation, convertibility and free trade are all elements.

learn.reallife: India chose gradual reform after 1991, opening sectors step by step. Comparing India's path with Russia's shock therapy is a classic debate in economics and political science classes.

games.title: Part of shock therapy?
items: Closing the economy to foreign trade

items.text: Shock therapy was promoted by the World Bank and the ___.
Valuable industries were sold cheaply in what was called the largest ___ sale in history.
Under shock therapy, collective farms were replaced by ___ farming.

quiz.q: What was 'shock therapy'?
options: A slow, step-by-step reform of socialism
A military strategy of the Warsaw Pact
A health scheme of the Soviet state
A sudden transition from socialism to democratic capitalism
quiz.explain: It was a rapid, all-at-once switch to a market economy and democracy.
steps: Asked: what shock therapy was.
Fact: it was a sudden transition from authoritarian socialism to democratic capitalism.
'Shock' means sudden, so it was not slow or step-by-step.
Answer: A sudden transition from socialism to democratic capitalism
quiz.mistake: Thinks shock therapy was gradual

quiz.q: Shock therapy was influenced mainly by:
options: The World Bank and the IMF
quiz.explain: These institutions pushed the model in post-communist states.
steps: Asked: who influenced shock therapy.
Fact: the model was influenced by the World Bank and the IMF.
The Warsaw Pact and NAM have nothing to do with it.
Answer: The World Bank and the IMF
quiz.mistake: Links shock therapy to communist or non-aligned bodies

quiz.q: Which was an element of shock therapy?
quiz.explain: Making the currency freely exchangeable was part of opening the economy.
steps: Elements of shock therapy: privatisation, free trade, FDI, financial openness, currency convertibility.
Collective farms, a ban on foreign investment and central planning are the old socialist ways.
So currency convertibility is an element.
Answer: Currency convertibility
quiz.mistake: Picks a socialist policy

quiz.q: Why was the privatisation under shock therapy called 'the largest garage sale in history'?
options: Old cars were sold to the West
State industries were sold off at very low prices
Citizens sold household goods to survive
The government bought back private firms
quiz.explain: Valuable assets went to private buyers far below their real worth.
steps: The phrase 'garage sale' means selling things very cheaply.
Fact: valuable state industries were sold to private buyers far below their real value.
So it means state industries were sold off at very low prices.
Answer: State industries were sold off at very low prices
quiz.mistake: Takes the phrase literally

quiz.q: Under shock therapy, the trade of post-communist countries was redirected towards:
quiz.explain: The old Soviet bloc trade links broke and trade shifted towards Western countries.
steps: Fact: shock therapy broke up the old Soviet bloc trade alliances.
Trade was redirected towards the West.
So the answer is the West.
Answer: The West
quiz.mistake: Thinks the old bloc trade alliances were strengthened

quiz.q: In shock therapy, what was to be the dominant pattern of ownership of property?
quiz.explain: The model made private ownership the main form of property.
steps: Fact: under shock therapy private ownership was to be the main pattern of property.
State and collective ownership belonged to the old Soviet model.
So private ownership.
Answer: Private ownership
quiz.mistake: Confuses the new system with the Soviet model

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Under shock therapy, collective farms were replaced by private farming. Reason (R): Shock therapy aimed at a complete shift to a capitalist economy.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true, and the aim of full capitalism explains the end of collective farms.
steps: A: true — collective farms were replaced by private farming.
R: true — shock therapy aimed at a complete shift to capitalism.
R explains A: private farming is part of that shift to capitalism.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Fails to connect the farming change with the goal of capitalism

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Shock therapy was a gradual transition to capitalism. Reason (R): It was promoted by the World Bank and IMF.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: it was sudden, hence 'shock'. R is true.
steps: A: false — shock therapy was sudden, not gradual ('shock').
R: true — it was promoted by the World Bank and IMF.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Ignores what the word 'shock' signals

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'Shock therapy? Did someone get an electric shock? What does it mean in politics?'
teach.praise: Zap! Shock therapy was the sudden jump from socialism to capitalism, pushed by the World Bank and IMF, with privatisation and free trade!
teach.nudge: Close! But was the change slow or sudden? And who pushed for it?

revise.summary: Shock therapy was the sudden switch from authoritarian socialism to democratic capitalism, influenced by the World Bank and IMF, with privatisation, free trade, currency convertibility and private farming.
remember: Private ownership became the main pattern of property
Elements: privatisation, collective farms replaced by private farming, free trade, FDI, currency convertibility
Trade was redirected towards the West
traps: Shock therapy was sudden, not gradual.
It did not strengthen collective farms.
'Garage sale' means state industries were sold at very low prices.

learn.hook: Imagine your family's lifetime savings losing almost all their value within months. For millions in 1990s Russia, that was not a nightmare but the morning news.
points: The value of the rouble, the Russian currency, declined dramatically. High inflation wiped out people's savings.
The collective farm system disintegrated, leaving people without food security, and Russia began to import food. The old trading structure broke down without an alternative.
The old system of social welfare was destroyed. Withdrawal of government subsidies pushed many into poverty, the middle class was pushed to the margins, and many intellectuals migrated.
A mafia emerged and controlled many economic activities. Privatisation created new disparities, and inequality between rich and poor grew sharply.
Democratic institutions were built in a hurry: most countries got a strong executive president and a weak parliament, and the judicial culture and independence were not established.

example.q: A pensioner in Moscow in 1993 finds that the savings that once bought a car now buy only a few loaves of bread. Which consequence of shock therapy explains this?
steps: Shock therapy freed prices and the currency.
The rouble fell steeply and inflation soared.
Savings held in roubles lost their value.
example.answer: Fall in the value of the rouble and high inflation

learn.reallife: India's own welfare safety nets, such as the public distribution system for food, show why the sudden loss of the Soviet welfare system hurt so many people.

games.title: Economic or political consequence?
items: Fall in the value of the rouble

games.title: True or false?
items: Shock therapy made Russia self-sufficient in food in the 1990s.
Food security collapsed and Russia began importing food.
Economic inequality grew under shock therapy.
The new democracies usually had very strong parliaments.
They had strong presidents and weak parliaments.
A mafia emerged and controlled many economic activities.
This was one of the social costs of the transition.

quiz.q: What happened to the rouble under shock therapy?
options: It became the world's reserve currency
It was replaced by the euro
quiz.explain: The currency fell sharply and inflation wiped out savings.
steps: Asked: what happened to the rouble.
Fact: the value of the rouble declined dramatically and inflation soared.
So its value declined dramatically.
Answer: Its value declined dramatically
quiz.mistake: Assumes opening up always strengthens a currency

quiz.q: Which consequence of shock therapy affected food security?
options: Disintegration of the collective farm system
quiz.explain: As collective farms broke up, food security collapsed and Russia began importing food.
steps: Asked: which consequence hit food security.
Fact: the collective farm system disintegrated, leaving people without food security.
Russia then began to import food.
Answer: Disintegration of the collective farm system
quiz.mistake: Thinks privatised farming immediately raised output

quiz.q: The political institutions built after communism usually had:
options: A strong executive president and a weak parliament
A strong parliament and no president
Rule by the Communist Party alone
quiz.explain: Constitutions drafted in a hurry gave presidents wide powers.
steps: Fact: democratic institutions were built in a hurry after communism.
Most countries got a strong executive president.
Parliaments were weak, so: a strong executive president and a weak parliament.
Answer: A strong executive president and a weak parliament
quiz.mistake: Assumes new democracies were balanced from the start

quiz.q: Which social consequence followed shock therapy?
options: Rise of a mafia and widening inequality
quiz.explain: Privatisation created new disparities and organised crime grew.
steps: Fact: a mafia emerged and controlled many economic activities.
Privatisation created new disparities, so inequality grew.
So a rise of a mafia and widening inequality (not equal incomes or a stronger welfare state).
Answer: Rise of a mafia and widening inequality
quiz.mistake: Expects market reform to reduce inequality at once

quiz.q: Why were many people pushed into poverty under shock therapy?
options: Government subsidies were withdrawn and the welfare system collapsed
quiz.explain: Removing subsidies hit ordinary people hard.
steps: Fact: the old system of social welfare was destroyed.
Withdrawal of government subsidies pushed many into poverty.
So subsidies were withdrawn and the welfare system collapsed.
Answer: Government subsidies were withdrawn and the welfare system collapsed
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the role of the welfare system

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Savings of many Russians were wiped out in the 1990s. Reason (R): High inflation followed the fall in the value of the rouble.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; inflation and a falling rouble destroyed the value of savings.
steps: A: true — many Russians lost their savings in the 1990s.
R: true — high inflation followed the fall in the rouble's value.
R explains A: inflation wiped out the value of savings.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not connect inflation with loss of savings

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Judicial independence was firmly established in post-communist states. Reason (R): Democratic institutions there were built in a hurry.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false: judicial culture and independence were not established. R is true.
steps: A: false — judicial culture and independence were not established.
R: true — democratic institutions were built in a hurry.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Assumes new constitutions created strong courts at once

quiz.q: Case: An engineer and a professor from Russia take up jobs abroad in 1995 because their salaries became worthless. This reflects which consequence?
options: Decline of the middle class and migration of intellectuals
quiz.explain: The middle class was pushed to the margins and many skilled people migrated.
steps: The case: an engineer and a professor leave because their salaries became worthless.
Fact: the middle class was pushed to the margins and many intellectuals migrated.
So it shows the decline of the middle class and migration of intellectuals.
Answer: Decline of the middle class and migration of intellectuals
quiz.mistake: Misses the social cost to the educated middle class

teach.ask: Gappu sighs: 'After shock therapy, were people happier? What happened to them?'
teach.praise: Oh no! The rouble crashed, savings vanished, food ran short, inequality and a mafia grew, and parliaments stayed weak. Tough times!
teach.nudge: You told me about money. What happened to food, welfare and the new parliaments?

revise.summary: Shock therapy caused a dramatic fall of the rouble and inflation, loss of food security, collapse of welfare, a mafia and growing inequality, and hastily built institutions with strong presidents and weak parliaments.
focus: Economic and social consequences of shock therapy
remember: Rouble declined dramatically; inflation wiped out savings
Collective farms disintegrated; Russia began importing food
Strong executive president, weak parliament, no judicial independence
traps: Market reform did not reduce inequality at once; it widened it.
Judicial independence was not established.

topics.title: Tensions and conflicts after the break-up

learn.hook: The Cold War ended, but peace did not arrive everywhere. Across the former communist world, new borders sparked new wars.
points: In Russia, Chechnya and Dagestan saw violent secessionist movements. Moscow's response, including military bombings, led to serious human rights violations.
Yugoslavia broke apart into several provinces after 1991. Ethnic conflict followed in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and in Kosovo NATO intervened with bombing of Yugoslavia in 1999.
Tajikistan suffered a civil war that went on for about ten years, until 2001.
In Azerbaijan, local Armenians of Nagorno-Karabakh wanted to separate and join Armenia. In Georgia, two provinces demanded independence.
Central Asia's rich hydrocarbon (oil and gas) reserves attracted competition among outside powers, including Russia, China and the USA, and the region became a zone of rivalry.

example.q: Match each conflict to its country: Chechnya, Nagorno-Karabakh, Kosovo.
steps: Chechnya: secessionist movement inside Russia.
Nagorno-Karabakh: region in Azerbaijan claimed by local Armenians.
Kosovo: province of the former Yugoslavia, where NATO intervened.
example.answer: Chechnya - Russia; Nagorno-Karabakh - Azerbaijan; Kosovo - former Yugoslavia

learn.reallife: India buys oil and gas from many regions to keep fuel flowing for its railways, vehicles and power plants. That is why Central Asia's energy wealth matters to New Delhi too.

games.title: Match the conflict
pairs: Armenians in Azerbaijan seeking to join Armenia
Civil war lasting about ten years

games.title: True or false?
items: Chechnya and Dagestan saw secessionist movements in Russia.
Both regions saw violent separatist conflict.
It broke into several provinces amid ethnic conflict.
NATO intervened in Kosovo by bombing Yugoslavia.
Central Asia has no oil or gas.
It has rich hydrocarbon reserves that attract outside powers.

quiz.q: Which two regions of Russia saw violent secessionist movements after 1991?
quiz.explain: Chechnya and Dagestan are inside Russia; the others are separate states or provinces elsewhere.
steps: Asked: regions inside Russia with violent secessionist movements.
Fact: Chechnya and Dagestan saw such movements.
Kosovo and Bosnia are in former Yugoslavia; Latvia, Estonia, Georgia and Armenia are separate states.
Answer: Chechnya and Dagestan
quiz.mistake: Names places outside Russia

quiz.q: Nagorno-Karabakh is a region where local Armenians wanted to separate from:
quiz.explain: The region lies in Azerbaijan; its Armenian population sought to join Armenia.
steps: Fact: Nagorno-Karabakh lies in Azerbaijan.
Its local Armenians wanted to separate and join Armenia.
So they wanted to separate from Azerbaijan.
Answer: Azerbaijan
quiz.mistake: Places the dispute in the wrong country

quiz.q: NATO intervened with bombing in 1999 over the conflict in:
quiz.explain: The Kosovo crisis in Yugoslavia led to NATO's bombing of Yugoslavia.
steps: Fact: in Kosovo, a province of the former Yugoslavia, NATO bombed Yugoslavia in 1999.
Chechnya and Tajikistan were conflicts in the former USSR without NATO bombing.
So Kosovo.
Answer: Kosovo
quiz.mistake: Confuses Balkan conflicts with those in former Soviet republics

quiz.q: Which former Soviet republic saw a civil war that lasted about ten years, until 2001?
quiz.explain: Tajikistan's civil war ran for about a decade.
steps: Asked: the republic with a civil war of about ten years, till 2001.
Fact: Tajikistan suffered that civil war.
So Tajikistan.
Answer: Tajikistan
quiz.mistake: Guesses a better-known republic

quiz.q: Why has Central Asia become a zone of competition among outside powers?
options: It has rich oil and gas reserves
It has the world's largest population
It is home to the UN headquarters
quiz.explain: Its hydrocarbon wealth attracts Russia, China, the USA and others.
steps: Fact: Central Asia has rich hydrocarbon (oil and gas) reserves.
These attract Russia, China, the USA and others.
So it is a zone of competition because of its oil and gas.
Answer: It has rich oil and gas reserves
quiz.mistake: Overlooks the role of energy resources

quiz.q: The break-up of Yugoslavia led to ethnic conflict in:
quiz.explain: Bosnia-Herzegovina, a former Yugoslav province, saw ethnic conflict.
steps: Fact: Yugoslavia broke apart after 1991, and ethnic conflict followed in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Finland, Uzbekistan and Poland were never part of Yugoslavia.
So Bosnia-Herzegovina.
Answer: Bosnia-Herzegovina
quiz.mistake: Picks a country that was never part of Yugoslavia

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Moscow's handling of the Chechen rebellion drew criticism. Reason (R): Its military bombings led to many human rights violations.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both true; the human rights violations explain the criticism.
steps: A: true — Moscow's handling of Chechnya was criticised.
R: true — its military bombings led to serious human rights violations.
R explains A: the violations are why it drew criticism.
Answer: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Does not see why the response was criticised

quiz.q: Assertion (A): All former communist states moved peacefully to democracy after 1991. Reason (R): Several regions witnessed civil wars and secessionist movements.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false, as the many conflicts show. R is true.
steps: A: false — the change was not peaceful everywhere.
R: true — Chechnya, Tajikistan, Yugoslavia and others saw civil wars and secessionist movements.
So A is false, but R is true.
Answer: A is false, but R is true
quiz.mistake: Assumes the end of the Cold War brought peace everywhere

teach.ask: Gappu is worried: 'Didn't everyone become peaceful friends once the Cold War ended?'
teach.praise: Hmm, so new wars broke out in Chechnya, Bosnia, Kosovo and Tajikistan, and Central Asia's oil drew rival powers. Not so peaceful after all!
teach.nudge: You mentioned Russia. What about Yugoslavia, and why do big powers care about Central Asia?

revise.summary: After the break-up, conflicts broke out: secessionism in Chechnya and Dagestan, the break-up of Yugoslavia with conflict in Bosnia and NATO bombing over Kosovo (1999), Tajikistan's civil war, Nagorno-Karabakh, and rivalry over Central Asian oil and gas.
focus: Why Central Asia became a zone of rivalry
remember: Chechnya and Dagestan: inside Russia
Nagorno-Karabakh: region in Azerbaijan claimed by local Armenians
Kosovo: NATO bombed Yugoslavia in 1999; Tajikistan civil war till 2001
traps: Kosovo and Bosnia are in former Yugoslavia, not the former USSR.
The end of the Cold War did not bring peace everywhere.

learn.hook: Generations of Indians grew up with Russian picture books and Soviet-built steel plants, while Russians hummed Raj Kapoor's songs. That friendship had to be rebuilt after 1991.
points: During the Cold War India and the USSR were close: the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation was signed in August 1971. The USSR backed India on Kashmir at the UN and helped with steel plants, defence equipment and culture.

India has kept good relations with all post-communist countries, and its strongest ties are with Russia. The two share a vision of a multipolar world: several powers coexisting, collective security, negotiated settlement of disputes and decision-making through bodies like the UN.

More than 80 agreements were signed under the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of 2001. India is one of the biggest buyers of Russian arms, and Russia has helped India's nuclear energy and space programmes.
For India, Russia matters for its stand on Kashmir, energy supplies, sharing information on terrorism, access to Central Asia, and balancing relations with China.
India also builds ties with energy-rich Central Asian states such as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan, to diversify its energy sources and improve connectivity.

example.q: Exam-style: List two reasons why Russia is important for India and one reason why India is important for Russia.
steps: Russia for India: support on Kashmir; energy supplies.
Also: access to Central Asia, intelligence on terrorism, balancing ties with China.
India for Russia: one of the largest markets for Russian arms.
example.answer: Kashmir support and energy for India; a big arms market for Russia

learn.reallife: Fighter jets of the Indian Air Force, the Kudankulam nuclear power plant in Tamil Nadu and joint space work all show how deep India-Russia cooperation runs.

quiz.q: In which year did India and the USSR sign the Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation?
quiz.explain: It was signed in August 1971, months before the Bangladesh war.
steps: Asked: the year of the Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation.
Fact: it was signed in August 1971.
1962 and 1991 are other events, so they do not fit.
Answer: 1971
quiz.mistake: Links the treaty to the 1962 war or the end of the USSR

quiz.q: India-Russia relations rest on a shared vision of:
options: A unipolar world led by one power
A world without any international organisations
quiz.explain: Both favour several powers coexisting, collective security and decisions through the UN.
steps: Fact: India and Russia share a vision of a multipolar world.
That means several powers coexisting and decisions through bodies like the UN.
So a multipolar world order, not a unipolar one.
Answer: A multipolar world order
quiz.mistake: Thinks India backs a unipolar order

quiz.q: Over 80 bilateral agreements were signed as part of the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement of:
quiz.explain: The Strategic Agreement dates from 2001.
steps: Fact: more than 80 agreements were signed under the Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement.
That agreement dates from 2001.
1971 is the earlier friendship treaty, a tempting wrong choice.
Answer: 2001
quiz.mistake: Confuses it with the 1971 treaty

quiz.q: Why is India important for Russia?
options: India supplies Russia with most of its oil
India is one of the largest buyers of Russian arms
quiz.explain: India is a major market for Russian defence equipment.
steps: Asked: why India matters to Russia.
Fact: India is one of the biggest buyers of Russian arms.
India is not Russia's oil supplier or a NATO member.
Answer: India is one of the largest buyers of Russian arms
quiz.mistake: Reverses the energy relationship

quiz.q: Which of these is a reason why Russia is important for India?
options: Access to Central Asia and energy supplies
quiz.explain: Russia matters for energy, Central Asian access, Kashmir and balancing China.
steps: Fact: Russia matters to India for Kashmir, energy, terrorism information, access to Central Asia and balancing China.
India and Russia do not share a border, and Russia is not in SAARC.
So access to Central Asia and energy supplies.
Answer: Access to Central Asia and energy supplies
quiz.mistake: Assumes Russia and India share a border

quiz.q: India seeks partnership with Central Asian states such as Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan mainly for:
quiz.explain: These states are rich in oil and gas, so India seeks energy ties.
steps: Fact: Kazakhstan and Turkmenistan are energy-rich Central Asian states.
India builds ties to diversify energy sources and improve connectivity.
So energy and connectivity.
Answer: Energy and connectivity
quiz.mistake: Overlooks Central Asia's hydrocarbon wealth

quiz.q: Assertion (A): India keeps good relations with all post-communist countries. Reason (R): The strongest of these relations is with Russia.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Both statements are true, but R does not explain A; the strength of ties with Russia is not the reason India is friendly with all.
steps: A: true — India keeps good relations with all post-communist countries.
R: true — its strongest ties are with Russia.
But R does not explain A: strong ties with one country are not the reason for good ties with all.
Answer: Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
quiz.mistake: Treats two related facts as cause and effect

quiz.q: Case: An Indian diplomat says, 'We want many centres of power, decisions through the UN and disputes settled by talks.' Which country shares this vision most closely, according to your book?
quiz.explain: India and Russia both favour a multipolar world with collective decision-making.
steps: The diplomat wants many centres of power, UN decisions and disputes settled by talks.
Fact: India and Russia share this vision of a multipolar world.
The USA of the 1990s was the unipolar power, so the answer is Russia.
Answer: Russia
quiz.mistake: Picks the unipolar power of the 1990s

revise.summary: India and the USSR were close during the Cold War (1971 treaty). India keeps good ties with all post-communist states, strongest with Russia, sharing a multipolar vision; Russia supplies arms and energy and helps on Kashmir and Central Asia.
focus: Why Russia matters to India and India to Russia
remember: Indo-Soviet Treaty of Peace, Friendship and Cooperation: August 1971
Indo-Russian Strategic Agreement 2001: over 80 agreements
India is one of the biggest buyers of Russian arms
traps: Don't confuse the 1971 treaty with the 2001 Strategic Agreement.
India backs a multipolar, not unipolar, world.
Two true related facts are not always cause and effect.
